claim: Overproduced yeast ribosomal protein Rpl26 fails to assemble into ribosomes and is degraded in the nucleus/nucleolus by a ubiquitin-proteasome system quality control pathway comprising the E2 enzymes Ubc4/Ubc5 and the ubiquitin ligase Tom1.
source: Overproduced yeast ribosomal protein (RP) Rpl26 fails to assemble into ribosomes and is degraded in the nucleus/nucleolus by a ubiquitin-proteasome system quality control pathway comprising the E2 enzymes Ubc4/Ubc5 and the ubiquitin ligase Tom1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing accumulation of Rpl26aFLAG in tom1∆ and ubc4∆ cells, loss of ubiquitination in these mutants, and localization studies.

claim: tom1 cells show reduced ubiquitination of multiple ribosomal proteins.
source: tom1 cells show reduced ubiquitination of multiple RPs, exceptional accumulation of detergent-insoluble proteins including multiple RPs, and hypersensitivity to imbalances in production of RPs and rRNA, indicative of a profound perturbation to proteostasis.
evidence: This is supported by GlyGly profiling data showing decreased ubiquitination of ribosomal proteins in tom1∆ cells.

claim: tom1 cells show exceptional accumulation of detergent-insoluble proteins including multiple ribosomal proteins.
source: tom1 cells show reduced ubiquitination of multiple RPs, exceptional accumulation of detergent-insoluble proteins including multiple RPs, and hypersensitivity to imbalances in production of RPs and rRNA, indicative of a profound perturbation to proteostasis.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of detergent-insoluble fractions showing enrichment of ribosomal proteins in tom1∆ cells.

claim: tom1 cells show hypersensitivity to imbalances in production of ribosomal proteins and rRNA.
source: tom1 cells show reduced ubiquitination of multiple RPs, exceptional accumulation of detergent-insoluble proteins including multiple RPs, and hypersensitivity to imbalances in production of RPs and rRNA, indicative of a profound perturbation to proteostasis.
evidence: This is supported by growth assays showing synthetic growth defects when tom1CA is combined with mutations affecting ribosome biogenesis.

claim: Tom1 directly ubiquitinates unassembled ribosomal proteins primarily via residues that are concealed in mature ribosomes.
source: Tom1 directly ubiquitinates unassembled RPs primarily via residues that are concealed in mature ribosomes.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assays, structural analysis of ubiquitination sites, and mutagenesis experiments with Rpl26a and Rpl4.

claim: A similar pathway mediated by the Tom1 homolog Huwe1 restricts accumulation of overexpressed hRpl26 in human cells.
source: A similar pathway, mediated by the Tom1 homolog Huwe1, restricts accumulation of overexpressed hRpl26 in human cells.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that knockdown or knockout of HUWE1 enables accumulation of overexpressed hRpl26FLAG in human cells.

claim: ERISQ is a key element of the quality control machinery that sustains protein homeostasis and cellular fitness in eukaryotes.
source: We propose that ERISQ is a key element of the quality control machinery that sustains protein homeostasis and cellular fitness in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Defects in cellular machinery that governs protein quality control cause multiple human diseases including multisystem proteinopathy.
source: Defects in the cellular machinery that governs PQC cause multiple human diseases including multisystem proteinopathy (Brandmeir et al., 2008; Watts et al., 2004) and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) (Johnson et al., 2010; Kabashi and Durham, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Defects in cellular machinery that governs protein quality control cause Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS).
source: Defects in the cellular machinery that governs PQC cause multiple human diseases including multisystem proteinopathy (Brandmeir et al., 2008; Watts et al., 2004) and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) (Johnson et al., 2010; Kabashi and Durham, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Multiple myeloma cells exhibit heightened dependency on protein quality control pathways, which underlies their hypersensitivity to proteasome inhibitors.
source: Other diseases, such as cancer, can exhibit heightened dependency on PQC pathways, which underlies the hypersensitivity of multiple myeloma cells to proteasome inhibitors (Cenci et al., 2012; Deshaies, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis is an intricate process involving many chaperones and assembly factors.
source: Ribosome biogenesis is an intricate process involving many chaperones and assembly factors (Kressler et al., 2010; Warner, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribosomal proteins made in excess over rRNA and other ribosomal proteins are among the most rapidly degraded proteins in eukaryotic cells.
source: Ribosomal proteins made in excess over rRNA and other ribosomal proteins are among the most rapidly degraded proteins in eukaryotic cells (Abovich et al., 1985; Dephoure et al., 2014; Gorenstein and Warner, 1977; Torres et al., 2010, 2007; Warner, 1977), suggesting that proper coordination of synthesis and assembly is critical.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Newly-synthesized human ribosomal proteins are subject to degradation by the proteasome in the nucleolus.
source: Newly-synthesized human ribosomal proteins are subject to degradation by the proteasome in the nucleolus (Lam et al., 2007), and we recently found that overexpressed yeast ribosomal proteins that fail to assemble are conjugated with ubiquitin and degraded by the proteasome in the nucleus (Sung et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Overexpressed yeast ribosomal proteins that fail to assemble are conjugated with ubiquitin and degraded by the proteasome in the nucleus.
source: Newly-synthesized human ribosomal proteins are subject to degradation by the proteasome in the nucleolus (Lam et al., 2007), and we recently found that overexpressed yeast ribosomal proteins that fail to assemble are conjugated with ubiquitin and degraded by the proteasome in the nucleus (Sung et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Insoluble material that accumulates upon transient inhibition of the proteasome in yeast is strongly enriched for ribosomal proteins.
source: Insoluble material that accumulates upon transient inhibition of the proteasome in yeast is strongly enriched for ribosomal proteins (Sung et al., 2016), pointing to PQC of unassembled ribosomal proteins as a major pathway of proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Rpl26aFLAG accumulates to high levels in tom1∆ and ubc4∆ cells upon overexpression from the GAL10 promoter.
source: Notably, Rpl26aFLAG accumulated to high levels in tom1∆ and ubc4∆ cells (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: Ubc4 is an ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2) that is paralogous to and functionally redundant with Ubc5.
source: Ubc4 is an ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2) that is paralogous to and functionally redundant with Ubc5 (Seufert and Jentsch, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Ubiquitinated Rpl26aFLAG was detected in pre9∆ but not in ubc4∆ubc5∆pre9∆ cells.
source: Ubiquitinated Rpl26aFLAG was detected in pre9∆ but not in ubc4∆ubc5∆pre9∆ cells (Figure 1B), indicating that Ubc4/Ubc5 promote ubiquitination of excess Rpl26a.
evidence: This claim is supported by UBA pull-down data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ubc4/Ubc5 promote ubiquitination of excess Rpl26a.
source: Ubiquitinated Rpl26aFLAG was detected in pre9∆ but not in ubc4∆ubc5∆pre9∆ cells (Figure 1B), indicating that Ubc4/Ubc5 promote ubiquitination of excess Rpl26a.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing loss of ubiquitination in the double mutant.

claim: Tom1 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase of the HECT (homologous to E6AP C terminus) family.
source: Tom1 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase of the HECT (homologous to E6AP C terminus) family.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Tom1.

claim: Tom1 E3 activity is required for repression of overexpressed Rpl26aFLAG.
source: Using these strains, we established that Tom1 E3 activity was required for repression (Figure 1C) and ubiquitination (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) of overexpressed Rpl26aFLAG.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing accumulation of Rpl26aFLAG in tom1CA mutant cells.

claim: Tom1 E3 activity is required for ubiquitination of overexpressed Rpl26aFLAG.
source: Using these strains, we established that Tom1 E3 activity was required for repression (Figure 1C) and ubiquitination (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) of overexpressed Rpl26aFLAG.
evidence: This claim is supported by UBA pull-down data showing loss of ubiquitination in tom1CA mutant cells.

claim: Rpl26aFLAG co-immunoprecipitates with 3×HATom1.
source: Rpl26aFLAG was co-immunoprecipitated with 3×HATom1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Wild type 3×HATom1 immunoprecipitates ubiquitinate co-precipitated Rpl26aFLAG upon addition of an ubiquitination cocktail.
source: Upon addition of an ubiquitination cocktail, immunoprecipitations of wild type but not mutant 3×HATom1 ubiquitinated co-precipitated Rpl26aFLAG (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data.

claim: The activity defect of the 3×HATom1CA immunoprecipitate was complemented by adding 3×HATom1 but not 3×HATom1CA prior to the ubiquitination reaction.
source: Importantly, the activity defect of the 3×HATom1CA immunoprecipitate was complemented by adding 3×HATom1 but not 3×HATom1CA prior to the ubiquitination reaction (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Mutant tom1CA cells accumulate unassembled Rpl26aFLAG that co-fractionates with 3×HATom1CA in sucrose gradient fractionation.
source: Mutant tom1CA cells, like cells treated with the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib (Sung et al., 2016), accumulated unassembled Rpl26aFLAG that co-fractionated with 3×HATom1CA (Figure 2A; note that 3×HATom1 and 3×HATom1CA fractionated similarly).
evidence: This claim is supported by sucrose gradient fractionation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of 3×HATom1 or 3×HATom1CA with Rpl26aFLAG was only detected in low MW fractions.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation of 3×HATom1 or 3×HATom1CA with Rpl26aFLAG was only detected in these low MW fractions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from fractionated samples shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Ubiquitinated Rpl26aFLAG detected in low MW fractions from bortezomib-treated cells was almost entirely lost from tom1CA cells.
source: Moreover, ubiquitinated Rpl26aFLAG detected in low MW fractions from bortezomib-treated cells was almost entirely lost from tom1CA cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by UBA pull-down data from fractionated samples shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tom1 localizes to the nucleus and nucleolus.
source: Consistent with the reported localization of Tom1 (Huh et al., 2003), Rpl26aFLAG or Rpl26aGFP that accumulated upon their transient overexpression in tom1CA cells were found in the nucleus and nucleolus (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and is consistent with the localization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Rpl26aFLAG or Rpl26aGFP that accumulated upon their transient overexpression in tom1CA cells were found in the nucleus and nucleolus.
source: Consistent with the reported localization of Tom1 (Huh et al., 2003), Rpl26aFLAG or Rpl26aGFP that accumulated upon their transient overexpression in tom1CA cells were found in the nucleus and nucleolus (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Overexpressed Rpl26a failed to assemble into ribosomes and was directly bound and ubiquitinated by Tom1 in the nuclear/nucleolar compartments.
source: Taken together, these data provide strong evidence that overexpressed Rpl26a failed to assemble into ribosomes and was directly bound and ubiquitinated by Tom1 in the nuclear/nucleolar compartments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from fractionation, co-immunoprecipitation, ubiquitination, and localization experiments.

claim: Deletion of TOM1 enabled increased accumulation of at least seven of eight ectopically overexpressed ribosomal proteins.
source: Similar to what we observed with bortezomib (Sung et al., 2016), deletion of TOM1 enabled increased accumulation of at least seven of them (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mass spectrometry of 3xHATom1 immunoprecipitates from bortezomib-treated cells revealed enrichment for several ribosomal proteins, including Rpl26b.
source: Mass spectrometry of 3xHATom1 immunoprecipitates from bortezomib-treated cells revealed enrichment for several ribosomal proteins, including Rpl26b (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ribosomal proteins are commonly identified in purified ubiquitin conjugates.
source: Ribosomal proteins are commonly identified in purified ubiquitin conjugates (Mayor et al., 2007, 2005; Peng et al., 2003) or in ubiquitination site mapping experiments that rely on purification of the GlyGly dipeptide that remains attached to a lysine side chain following digestion of an ubiquitin conjugate with trypsin (Kim et al., 2011; Lesmantavicius et al., 2014; Porras-Yakushi and Hess, 2014; Porras-Yakushi et al., 2015; Sarraf et al., 2013; Swaney et al., 2013; Udeshi et al., 2013b; Wagner et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: GlyGly profiling of tom1∆ and TOM1 cells revealed 1980 unique ubiquitination sites in 920 distinct proteins, of which 972 unique sites in 532 proteins were quantified.
source: Analysis of three biological replicates (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 3B) revealed 1980 unique ubiquitination sites in 920 distinct proteins, of which 972 unique sites in 532 proteins were quantified.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from GlyGly profiling experiments.

claim: All three tom1∆ biological replicates exhibited lower overall ubiquitination than wild type.
source: All three tom1∆ biological replicates exhibited lower overall ubiquitination than wild type, suggesting a major role for Tom1 in PQC.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of GlyGly profiling data.

claim: Of the 141 ubiquitination sites that exhibited a ≥two-fold decrease in ubiquitination in tom1∆, 51 (36%) were in ribosomal proteins.
source: Of the 141 sites that exhibited a ≥two-fold decrease in ubiquitination in tom1∆, 51 (36%) were in ribosomal proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of GlyGly profiling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Of the ubiquitinated peptides derived from ribosomal proteins, >50% (51 of 101) decreased in abundance in tom1∆.
source: Moreover, of the ubiquitinated peptides derived from ribosomal proteins, >50% (51 of 101) decreased in abundance in tom1∆.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of GlyGly profiling data.

claim: Of 837 non-ribosomal ubiquitination sites identified, only 11% decreased in abundance in tom1∆.
source: By comparison, of 837 non-ribosomal sites identified, only 11% decreased in abundance in tom1∆.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of GlyGly profiling data.

claim: The reduction in ribosomal ubiquitin conjugates in tom1∆ was not due to reduction in total ribosomal protein levels.
source: SILAC analysis of the unfractionated cell lysates indicated that the reduction in ribosomal ubiquitin conjugates in tom1∆ was not due to reduction in total ribosomal protein levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC analysis of total protein levels shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of the GlyGly profiling data confirmed that ubiquitination of ribosomal proteins, particularly those of the large (60S) subunit, was disproportionately impacted by loss of Tom1.
source: Gene ontology analysis of the GlyGly profiling data confirmed that ubiquitination of ribosomal proteins (Figure 3C), particularly those of the large (60S) subunit (Figure 3D), was disproportionately impacted by loss of Tom1.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of GlyGly profiling data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The strong effects on ribosomal protein ubiquitination seen in tom1∆ cells were due specifically to loss of Tom1's E3 activity.
source: To address whether the strong effects on ribosomal protein ubiquitination seen in tom1∆ cells were due specifically to loss of Tom1's E3 activity, the GlyGly SILAC analysis was repeated with WT and tom1CA cells. Quantitative analysis of the data confirmed a disproportionate loss of ribosomal protein ubiquitination (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GlyGly profiling data comparing WT and tom1CA cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Detergent-insoluble proteins, including Rpl1 and Rpl3, were greatly increased in tom1∆ cells compared to WT cells.
source: Detergent-insoluble proteins, including Rpl1 and Rpl3, were greatly increased in tom1∆ cells compared to WT cells (Figure 3F, Pellet).
evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining and Western blot analysis of detergent-insoluble fractions shown in Figure 3F.

claim: High accumulation of insoluble proteins in tom1∆ cells was evident regardless of the method or buffer employed for cell lysis.
source: High accumulation of insoluble proteins in tom1∆ cells was evident regardless of the method or buffer employed for cell lysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A testing different lysis conditions.

claim: The insoluble proteins that exhibited the largest increase in tom1∆ cells were ribosomal proteins including Rpl1 and Rpl3.
source: The insoluble proteins that exhibited the largest increase in tom1∆ cells were ribosomal proteins including Rpl1 and Rpl3 (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, and Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Ribosomal proteins, including those of both the 60S and 40S subunits, comprise the major class of aggregating proteins in tom1∆ cells.
source: Gene ontology analysis (Figure 3H) and a plot of the top 20 detergent-insoluble proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C) indicated that ribosomal proteins, including those of both the 60S and 40S subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D) comprise the major class of aggregating proteins in tom1∆ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3H and supplementary figures.

claim: Two positively-charged clusters in Rpl26 – RRKARK (amino acids 12–17) and a patch formed by R27, R28, R51, and R52 – mediate binding to 5.8S rRNA and assembly into ribosomes.
source: Two positively-charged clusters in Rpl26 – RRKARK (amino acids 12–17) and a patch formed by R27, R28, R51, and R52 – mediate binding to 5.8S rRNA and assembly into ribosomes (Babiano et al., 2012) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and is illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Some mutants of Rpl26a with mutations in rRNA-binding residues exhibited even less accumulation than overexpressed WT Rpl26aFLAG.
source: We mutated various combinations of these residues to glutamate and observed that some mutants exhibited even less accumulation than overexpressed WT Rpl26aFLAG (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Rpl26-4EFLAG (R12E, R13E, R16E, K17E) did not accumulate or assemble into ribosomes in rpl26a∆rpl26b∆ cells.
source: Unlike WT Rpl26aFLAG, Rpl26-4EFLAG(R12E, R13E, R16E, K17E) did not accumulate or assemble into ribosomes in rpl26a∆rpl26b∆ cells (Figure 4C, top panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by sucrose gradient fractionation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Upon inhibition of the proteasome with MG132 or bortezomib, Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated and was detected in the low MW fractions of a sucrose gradient.
source: However, upon inhibition of the proteasome with MG132 or bortezomib, Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and was detected in the low MW fractions of a sucrose gradient (Figure 4C, bottom panels), where it was ubiquitinated, albeit to a lesser extent than unassembled WT Rpl26aFLAG (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by sucrose gradient fractionation data shown in Figure 4C and supplementary data.

claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG was ubiquitinated to a lesser extent than unassembled WT Rpl26aFLAG.
source: However, upon inhibition of the proteasome with MG132 or bortezomib, Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and was detected in the low MW fractions of a sucrose gradient (Figure 4C, bottom panels), where it was ubiquitinated, albeit to a lesser extent than unassembled WT Rpl26aFLAG (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by UBA pull-down data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG exhibited poor association with 3xHATom1.
source: Strikingly, Rpl26a-4EFLAG exhibited poor association with 3xHATom1 (Figure 4E) and showed only very weak accumulation in tom1∆ (Figure 4F), suggesting that it is not primarily a Tom1 substrate but is re-directed to another QC pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG showed only very weak accumulation in tom1∆.
source: Strikingly, Rpl26a-4EFLAG exhibited poor association with 3xHATom1 (Figure 4E) and showed only very weak accumulation in tom1∆ (Figure 4F), suggesting that it is not primarily a Tom1 substrate but is re-directed to another QC pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG is not primarily a Tom1 substrate but is re-directed to another QC pathway.
source: Strikingly, Rpl26a-4EFLAG exhibited poor association with 3xHATom1 (Figure 4E) and showed only very weak accumulation in tom1∆ (Figure 4F), suggesting that it is not primarily a Tom1 substrate but is re-directed to another QC pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the poor association with Tom1 and weak accumulation in tom1∆ cells.

claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated in doa10 mutants.
source: Consistent with this idea, Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated in doa10 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The failure of Rpl26a-4EFLAG to be targeted by Tom1 was not due to a defect in its nuclear localization.
source: The failure of Rpl26a-4EFLAG to be targeted by Tom1 was not due to a defect in its nuclear localization (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Residues of Rpl26a that mediate interactions with rRNA and are buried when incorporated into the ribosome are required for ubiquitination by Tom1 when Rpl26a fails to assemble.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that residues of Rpl26a that mediate interactions with rRNA and are buried when incorporated into the ribosome are also required for ubiquitination by Tom1 when Rpl26a fails to assemble.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined mutagenesis and ubiquitination data for Rpl26a.

claim: Upon its synthesis, Rpl4 binds the dedicated chaperone Acl4.
source: Upon its synthesis, Rpl4 binds the dedicated chaperone Acl4. The Rpl4–Acl4 then recruits the karyopherin Kap104, for import into the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on Rpl4 assembly.

claim: The Rpl4–Acl4 complex recruits the karyopherin Kap104 for import into the nucleus.
source: Upon its synthesis, Rpl4 binds the dedicated chaperone Acl4. The Rpl4–Acl4 then recruits the karyopherin Kap104, for import into the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on Rpl4 assembly.

claim: K55 and K308 of Rpl4, whose ubiquitinations exhibited the strongest dependence on Tom1, contact rRNA and are not accessible for modification in the mature ribosome.
source: The crystal structure of the ribosome indicates that K55 and K308, whose ubiquitinations exhibited the strongest dependence on Tom1, contact rRNA and are not accessible for modification in the mature ribosome (Ben-Shem et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the ribosome crystal structure and GlyGly profiling data.

claim: The crystal structure of the Acl4–Rpl4 complex revealed that Acl4 conceals K55.
source: Interestingly, the crystal structure of the Acl4–Rpl4 complex revealed that Acl4 conceals K55, and a structural model of Kap104 docked to Acl4–Rpl4 indicates that it protects K308 and K338.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the Acl4–Rpl4 complex.

claim: A structural model of Kap104 docked to Acl4–Rpl4 indicates that it protects K308 and K338.
source: Interestingly, the crystal structure of the Acl4–Rpl4 complex revealed that Acl4 conceals K55, and a structural model of Kap104 docked to Acl4–Rpl4 indicates that it protects K308 and K338.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling of the Acl4–Rpl4–Kap104 complex.

claim: Upon import of Rpl4–Acl4–Kap104 into the nucleus, Kap104 is dissociated through the action of Ran-GTP.
source: Upon import of Rpl4–Acl4–Kap104 into the nucleus, Kap104 is dissociated through the action of Ran-GTP (Kressler et al., 2012)(F. H. and A. H., submitted).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 3xHATom1 immunoprecipitates readily ubiquitinated Rpl4 in binary Acl4–Rpl4 complexes but not in ternary Acl4–Rpl4–ctKap104 complexes.
source: 3xHATom1 immunoprecipitates readily ubiquitinated Rpl4 in binary Acl4–Rpl4 complexes but not in ternary Acl4–Rpl4–ctKap104 complexes, despite the fact that at least eight lysines of Rpl4 should remain exposed in the ternary complex (red circle, Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ubiquitination of Rpl4 within the binary Acl4–Rpl4 complex required its extended C-terminus because it was eliminated when the C-terminal region was truncated at residue 276.
source: Ubiquitination of Rpl4 within the binary complex required its extended C-terminus because it was eliminated when the C-terminal region was truncated at residue 276 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data with truncated Rpl4 shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Tom1 selectively recognizes and ubiquitinates ribosomal proteins via residues that are only accessible in the unassembled state.
source: These data, along with those on Rpl26a, suggest that Tom1 selectively recognizes and ubiquitinates ribosomal proteins via residues that are only accessible in the unassembled state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from Rpl26a and Rpl4 experiments.

claim: Of the 18 lysines from large subunit ribosomal proteins that could be observed in the 4V88 structure, 13 in the free 60S and 15 in the assembled 80S were not accessible to the probe.
source: Of the 18 lysines that could be observed in the 4V88 structure, 13 in the free 60S and 15 in the assembled 80S were not accessible to the probe (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Tom1-dependent ubiquitination events generally occur on ribosomal proteins prior to their assembly into the ribosome, on residues that normally are either buried in the ribosome, engage in salt bridges, or are otherwise shielded from contact.
source: Taken together, our data suggest strongly that Tom1-dependent ubiquitination events generally occur on ribosomal proteins prior to their assembly into the ribosome, on residues that normally are either buried in the ribosome, engage in salt bridges, or are otherwise shielded from contact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined structural and experimental data.

claim: tom1CA cells were extremely sensitive to constitutive overexpression of RPL26A from the GAL10 promoter.
source: First, tom1CA cells (but not WT cells) were extremely sensitive to constitutive overexpression of RPL26A (Figure 6A) but not RPL26A-4E (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) from the GAL10 promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: tom1CA cells were not sensitive to constitutive overexpression of RPL26A-4E from the GAL10 promoter.
source: First, tom1CA cells (but not WT cells) were extremely sensitive to constitutive overexpression of RPL26A (Figure 6A) but not RPL26A-4E (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) from the GAL10 promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Depletion of Rrn3, Rpa190, or Hmo1 caused a synthetic growth defect when combined with tom1CA.
source: Second, we created a situation in which ribosomal proteins as a group are made in excess of rRNA via depletion (using the auxin-inducible degron (AID) [Morawska and Ulrich, 2013]) of proteins involved in rRNA synthesis including Rrn3 (transcription factor for RNA polymerase I), Rpa190 (RNA polymerase I largest subunit) and Hmo1 (regulator of transcription by RNA polymerase I). Each of these depletions caused a synthetic growth defect when combined with tom1CA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The effect of combining hmo1∆ and tom1CA mutations was even more severe than depletion of Rrn3 or Rpa190 combined with tom1CA.
source: The effect of combining hmo1∆ and tom1CA mutations was even more severe (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Inactivation of TOM1 in an acl4∆ background caused a substantial synthetic growth defect.
source: Third, we manipulated cells such that assembly of a single ribosomal protein was impaired, via deletion of the Rpl4-selective chaperone Acl4 (Stelter et al., 2015). Inactivation of TOM1 in an acl4∆ background caused a substantial synthetic growth defect (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There was a massive increase in detergent-insoluble proteins when RNA Pol I transcription was diminished (hmo1∆tom1CA) in a tom1CA background.
source: Strikingly, there was a massive increase in detergent-insoluble proteins when RNA Pol I transcription was diminished (hmo1∆tom1CA; Figure 6D) or Rpl4 assembly was perturbed (acl4∆tom1CA; Figure 6E) in a tom1CA background.
evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was a massive increase in detergent-insoluble proteins when Rpl4 assembly was perturbed (acl4∆tom1CA) in a tom1CA background.
source: Strikingly, there was a massive increase in detergent-insoluble proteins when RNA Pol I transcription was diminished (hmo1∆tom1CA; Figure 6D) or Rpl4 assembly was perturbed (acl4∆tom1CA; Figure 6E) in a tom1CA background.
evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Deletions in 36 different genes encoding ribosomal proteins exhibit synthetic negative genetic interaction with tom1∆.
source: In addition to suppressors that map to stress response/chaperone pathways and genes involved in ribosome protein expression (PKA pathway), deletions in 36 different genes encoding ribosomal proteins exhibit synthetic negative genetic interaction with tom1∆ (Costanzo et al., 2010) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and is summarized in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Deletion of one of the two copies of RPS29 led to a synthetic growth defect in a tom1∆ mutant.
source: Consistent with this prediction, deletion of one of the two copies of RPS29 led to a synthetic growth defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) and enormous accumulation of insoluble proteins in a tom1∆ mutant (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Deletion of one of the two copies of RPS29 led to enormous accumulation of insoluble proteins in a tom1∆ mutant.
source: Consistent with this prediction, deletion of one of the two copies of RPS29 led to a synthetic growth defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) and enormous accumulation of insoluble proteins in a tom1∆ mutant (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Under unperturbed conditions, tom1∆ cells contained significantly greater amounts of insoluble proteins compared to doa10∆, hrd1∆, ltn1∆, san1∆, and ubr1∆ mutants.
source: Under unperturbed conditions, tom1∆ cells contained significantly greater amounts of insoluble proteins compared to these other PQC mutants (Figure 6G, Pellet), suggesting that ERISQ is a major player in maintaining proteostasis in yeast.
evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining of insoluble fractions from various PQC mutants shown in Figure 6G.

claim: ERISQ is a major player in maintaining proteostasis in yeast.
source: Under unperturbed conditions, tom1∆ cells contained significantly greater amounts of insoluble proteins compared to these other PQC mutants (Figure 6G, Pellet), suggesting that ERISQ is a major player in maintaining proteostasis in yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of insoluble protein accumulation in different PQC mutants.

claim: A significant fraction of newly-synthesized ribosomal proteins imported into the nucleus is degraded by the UPS in human cells.
source: A prior study in human cells demonstrated that a significant fraction of newly-synthesized ribosomal proteins imported into the nucleus is degraded by the UPS (Lam et al., 2007), suggesting that a PQC mechanism for unassembled ribosomal proteins is conserved in higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cells treated with proteasome inhibitors MG132 or bortezomib accumulated greater amounts of overexpressed hRpl26FLAG.
source: Cells treated with these proteasome inhibitors accumulated greater amounts of overexpressed hRpl26FLAG (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 1), consistent with the existence of a UPS pathway that degrades overexpressed ribosomal proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knockdown of Huwe1 by shRNA in T-REx-293 and HeLa cells enabled transient overexpression of hRpl26FLAG.
source: Knockdown of Huwe1 by shRNA (Thompson et al., 2014) in both T-REx-293 and HeLa cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—source data 2) and knockout of HUWE1 in HEK293T cells (Choe et al., 2016) (Figure 7C, Figure 7—source data 3) enabled transient overexpression of hRpl26FLAG.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Knockout of HUWE1 in HEK293T cells enabled transient overexpression of hRpl26FLAG.
source: Knockdown of Huwe1 by shRNA (Thompson et al., 2014) in both T-REx-293 and HeLa cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—source data 2) and knockout of HUWE1 in HEK293T cells (Choe et al., 2016) (Figure 7C, Figure 7—source data 3) enabled transient overexpression of hRpl26FLAG.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: hRpl26FLAG overexpressed in HUWE1 knockout cells was stable in a cycloheximide chase experiment.
source: Importantly, a cycloheximide chase experiment indicated that hRpl26FLAG overexpressed in HUWE1 knockout cells was stable (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: hRpl26FLAG was modified by HAubiquitin in control but not Huwe1-depleted cells.
source: IP/Western blot analysis performed under denaturing conditions revealed that hRpl26FLAG was modified by HAubiquitin in control but not Huwe1-depleted cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by IP/Western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Prior analysis of Huwe1-deficient cells by GlyGly profiling revealed reductions in the ubiquitination of multiple ribosomal proteins.
source: Consistent with this result, prior analysis of Huwe1-deficient cells by GlyGly profiling revealed reductions in the ubiquitination of multiple ribosomal proteins (Thompson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Nearly 40 years ago Jonathan Warner and colleagues showed that multiple ribosomal proteins are rapidly degraded in both yeast and HeLa cells when ribosomal RNA synthesis is inhibited.
source: Nearly 40 years ago Jonathan Warner and colleagues showed that multiple ribosomal proteins are rapidly degraded in both yeast and HeLa cells when ribosomal RNA synthesis is inhibited (Gorenstein and Warner, 1977; Warner, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Individual ribosomal proteins cannot be overexpressed from plasmids in yeast because the excess protein is rapidly degraded.
source: They and others went on to show that individual ribosomal proteins cannot be overexpressed from plasmids in yeast because the excess protein is rapidly degraded (Abovich et al., 1985; Warner et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribosome proteins are among the most abundant ubiquitin conjugates that accumulate in yeast cells with reduced proteasome activity.
source: Essentially no progress was made towards understanding the underlying mechanism, until it was shown that ribosomal proteins are among the most abundant ubiquitin conjugates that accumulate in yeast cells with reduced proteasome activity (Mayor et al., 2007, 2005), and that newly-synthesized ribosomal proteins are degraded by the proteasome in human nucleoli (Lam et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ubiquitin ligase Tom1 collaborates with the E2 enzymes Ubc4 and Ubc5 to broadly mediate degradation of unassembled ribosomal proteins in yeast.
source: In the work reported here, we shed additional light on this old puzzle by showing that the ubiquitin ligase Tom1 collaborates with the E2 enzymes Ubc4 and Ubc5 to broadly mediate degradation of unassembled ribosomal proteins in yeast.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For Tom1 to act upon ribosomal proteins, residues that are normally concealed in the mature ribosome must be accessible.
source: Although the exact structural basis for this discrimination remains to be determined, our analysis reveals that for Tom1 to act upon ribosomal proteins, residues that are normally concealed in the mature ribosome must be accessible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined experimental and structural data.

claim: Nearly 83% (15 of 18) of the major Tom1-dependent ubiquitination sites on 12 different ribosomal proteins are no longer available to Tom1 following incorporation into the 80S ribosome.
source: In addition, mapping of the major Tom1-dependent ubiquitination sites on the structure of the ribosome large subunit revealed that nearly 83% (15 of 18) of the sites on 12 different ribosomal proteins are no longer available to Tom1 following incorporation into the 80S ribosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of ubiquitination sites on the ribosome structure.

claim: A kinetic competition between Tom1 and rRNA for binding to ribosomal proteins newly arrived in the nucleolus determines whether proteins are assembled or degraded.
source: This suggests a very simple kinetic competition between Tom1 and rRNA for binding to ribosomal proteins newly arrived in the nucleolus. If the kinetic parameters for this race normally favor rRNA, the correct outcome would dominate and only those proteins that fail to assemble would be targeted.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the selectivity of Tom1 for unassembled ribosomal proteins.

claim: Tom1 has been implicated in the degradation of unassembled histones.
source: Tom1 has also been implicated in the degradation of unassembled histones (Singh et al., 2009), in which case a similar kinetic competition could apply.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The previously-described Tom1 substrates Dia2, Hht2, and Yra1 have pI values ranging from 9.3–12.
source: Although the domain employed by Tom1 to bind its substrates remains unknown, we note that the previously-described Tom1 substrates Dia2 (Kim and Koepp, 2012), Hht2 (Singh et al., 2009) and Yra1 (Iglesias et al., 2010) have pI values ranging from 9.3–12.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and knowledge of protein properties.

claim: Tom1, which is overall acidic (pI 4.8), may have a negatively-charged region that interacts electrostatically with basic substrates.
source: Thus, Tom1, which is overall acidic (pI 4.8) may have a negatively-charged region that interacts electrostatically with basic substrates.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that Tom1 substrates are basic.

claim: Human cells are unable to accumulate ribosomal proteins made in excess over rRNA due to rapid turnover.
source: Seminal studies from Warner indicated that human cells, like yeast, are unable to accumulate ribosomal proteins made in excess over rRNA due to rapid turnover (Warner, 1977), and subsequent proteomic studies revealed that a substantial fraction of newly-synthesized human ribosomal proteins are rapidly degraded by the proteasome (Lam et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both ubiquitination and degradation of excess hRpl26 require Huwe1.
source: To test whether the mechanism we described in yeast also operates in human cells, we first demonstrated that the human ortholog (hRpl26) of yeast Rpl26 fails to accumulate upon transient overexpression, and then established that both ubiquitination and degradation of excess hRpl26 require Huwe1, which is the closest human homolog of Tom1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing that knockdown or knockout of HUWE1 enables accumulation of hRpl26 and reduces its ubiquitination.

claim: Six of the top ten ubiquitination sites affected by Huwe1 depletion and seventeen of fifty-six that exhibited ≥two-fold decreased occupancy were from ribosomal proteins.
source: A recent proteome-wide profiling of ubiquitination sites that exhibit diminished occupancy upon depletion of Huwe1 revealed that, excluding Huwe1 itself, six of the top ten affected sites and seventeen of fifty-six that exhibited ≥two-fold decreased occupancy were from ribosomal proteins (Thompson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cells lacking Tom1 exhibit cell cycle arrest, nucleolar fragmentation, defective mRNA export from the nucleus, reduced Ngg1/Ada3-dependent transcription, reduced polysomes, and reduced rate of rRNA processing/maturation.
source: Cells lacking Tom1 exhibit a variety of phenotypes besides ERISQ including cell cycle arrest, nucleolar fragmentation, defective mRNA export from the nucleus, reduced Ngg1/Ada3-dependent transcription, reduced polysomes, reduced rate of rRNA processing/maturation (Duncan et al., 2000; Saleh et al., 1998; Tabb et al., 2001; Utsugi et al., 1999), and sensitivity to paromomycin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Cells lacking Tom1 exhibit sensitivity to paromomycin.
source: Cells lacking Tom1 exhibit a variety of phenotypes besides ERISQ including cell cycle arrest, nucleolar fragmentation, defective mRNA export from the nucleus, reduced Ngg1/Ada3-dependent transcription, reduced polysomes, reduced rate of rRNA processing/maturation (Duncan et al., 2000; Saleh et al., 1998; Tabb et al., 2001; Utsugi et al., 1999), and sensitivity to paromomycin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The defect in ERISQ is observed at temperatures that are permissive for growth of tom1 mutants.
source: We can rule out that ERISQ is an indirect consequence of cell cycle arrest, nucleolar fragmentation, defective mRNA export, or a reduced rate of rRNA processing, because the defect in ERISQ is observed at temperatures that are permissive for growth of tom1 mutants, whereas the other defects are only seen (or in the case of rRNA processing rate, is strongly enhanced) at the non-permissive temperature and thus are more likely to arise indirectly from exacerbation of a primary defect upon imposition of heat stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temperature-dependence of different phenotypes in tom1 mutants.

claim: Genetic reductions of protein kinase A activity suppress tom1∆.
source: However, the observation that genetic reductions of protein kinase A activity (which are predicted to diminish synthesis of ribosome proteins) suppress tom1∆ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) seems inconsistent with the idea that Tom1 plays a direct positive role in ribosome assembly.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: tom1CA mutants are unable to sustain growth upon overexpression of RPL26.
source: Specifically, tom1CA mutants are unable to sustain growth upon overexpression of RPL26, are sensitive to loss of the Rpl4-specific chaperone Acl4 (Stelter et al., 2015), are sensitive to reduction in expression (through deletion of one of two alleles) of a single ribosomal protein, and are hypersensitive to reduction of function in three different proteins involved in transcription by RNA polymerase I.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: tom1CA mutants are sensitive to loss of the Rpl4-specific chaperone Acl4.
source: Specifically, tom1CA mutants are unable to sustain growth upon overexpression of RPL26, are sensitive to loss of the Rpl4-specific chaperone Acl4 (Stelter et al., 2015), are sensitive to reduction in expression (through deletion of one of two alleles) of a single ribosomal protein, and are hypersensitive to reduction of function in three different proteins involved in transcription by RNA polymerase I.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: tom1CA mutants are sensitive to reduction in expression (through deletion of one of two alleles) of a single ribosomal protein.
source: Specifically, tom1CA mutants are unable to sustain growth upon overexpression of RPL26, are sensitive to loss of the Rpl4-specific chaperone Acl4 (Stelter et al., 2015), are sensitive to reduction in expression (through deletion of one of two alleles) of a single ribosomal protein, and are hypersensitive to reduction of function in three different proteins involved in transcription by RNA polymerase I.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: tom1CA mutants are hypersensitive to reduction of function in three different proteins involved in transcription by RNA polymerase I.
source: Specifically, tom1CA mutants are unable to sustain growth upon overexpression of RPL26, are sensitive to loss of the Rpl4-specific chaperone Acl4 (Stelter et al., 2015), are sensitive to reduction in expression (through deletion of one of two alleles) of a single ribosomal protein, and are hypersensitive to reduction of function in three different proteins involved in transcription by RNA polymerase I.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: tom1 mutants accumulate high levels of insoluble ribosomal proteins.
source: Moreover, tom1 mutants accumulate high levels of insoluble ribosomal proteins (which is consistent with their inability to degrade excess ribosomal proteins that may exist at any given point in time), and combining tom1 with a mutation that causes an imbalance in ribosome production (e.g. tom1CA acl4∆) leads to an enormous increase in insoluble protein, suggestive of a collapse in cellular proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of insoluble fractions presented in the manuscript.

claim: Combining tom1 with a mutation that causes an imbalance in ribosome production (e.g. tom1CA acl4∆) leads to an enormous increase in insoluble protein, suggestive of a collapse in cellular proteostasis.
source: Moreover, tom1 mutants accumulate high levels of insoluble ribosomal proteins (which is consistent with their inability to degrade excess ribosomal proteins that may exist at any given point in time), and combining tom1 with a mutation that causes an imbalance in ribosome production (e.g. tom1CA acl4∆) leads to an enormous increase in insoluble protein, suggestive of a collapse in cellular proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining of insoluble fractions from double mutants presented in the manuscript.

claim: Even the tom1∆ single mutant accumulates more insoluble protein than doa10∆, hrd1∆, ltn1∆, san1∆, or ubr1∆ mutants.
source: Notably, even the tom1∆ single mutant accumulates more insoluble protein than any other PQC mutant that we examined, including the ERAD mutants doa10∆ and hrd1∆ (Vembar and Brodsky, 2008), the ribosome QC mutant ltn1∆ (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010; Brandman et al., 2012; Defenouillere et al., 2013; Verma et al., 2013), the nuclear QC mutant san1∆ (Gardner et al., 2005), or the cytosolic QC mutant ubr1∆ (Eisele and Wolf, 2008; Heck et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of insoluble protein accumulation in different PQC mutants presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tom1 directly binds and ubiquitylates unassembled ribosome proteins.
source: Taken together with our observations that Tom1 directly binds and ubiquitylates unassembled ribosome proteins, these data point to a direct and critical role for Tom1 in the cellular proteostasis network.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In human cells, reduction of rRNA expression by low-dose actinomycin D treatment results in poor assembly of several ribosomal proteins including Rpl5, Rpl11, Rpl26, Rps7, and Rps14.
source: Regarding feedback mechanisms, it is interesting to note that in human cells, reduction of rRNA expression by low-dose actinomycin D treatment results in poor assembly of several ribosomal proteins including Rpl5 (Dai and Lu, 2004), Rpl11 (Lohrum et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2003), Rpl26 (Zhang et al., 2010), Rps7 (Chen et al., 2007) and Rps14 (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Unassembled ribosomal proteins bind to and titrate ubiquitin ligase Mdm2, which leads to stabilization and accumulation of the Mdm2 substrate p53.
source: These unassembled ribosomal proteins bind to and titrate ubiquitin ligase Mdm2, which leads to stabilization and accumulation of the Mdm2 substrate p53.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Mdm2-p53 feedback pathway provides a sensitive feedback loop to reduce cell growth in response to stresses that impede ribosome assembly.
source: This provides a sensitive feedback loop to reduce cell growth in response to stresses that impede ribosome assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of the Mdm2-p53 pathway.

claim: Dysfunctional ribosomal proteins and ribosome biogenesis has been linked to many diseases.
source: Dysfunctional ribosomal proteins and ribosome biogenesis has been linked to many diseases (Freed et al., 2010; Narla and Ebert, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One of the characteristic features of cancer is an increase in the overall rate of protein synthesis.
source: Particularly, given that one of the characteristic features of cancer is an increase in the overall rate of protein synthesis, it is clear that regulation of ribosome biogenesis is closely associated with tumor progression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: RNA Pol I activity is highly elevated in many cancer cells and it leads to the enlargement of the nucleolus, which has been used as a marker for cancer for over 100 years.
source: Consistent with this expectation, RNA Pol I activity is highly elevated in many cancer cells and it leads to the enlargement of the nucleolus, which has been used as a marker for cancer for over 100 years (Derenzini et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Two major human tumor suppressor proteins, pRB and p53, have been shown to repress the production of rRNA.
source: Furthermore, two major human tumor suppressor proteins, pRB and p53, have been shown to repress the production of rRNA and the loss of these factors cause an up-regulation of ribosome biogenesis in cancer tissues, consistent with a close relationship between cancer and ribosome synthesis (Montanaro et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The loss of pRB and p53 causes an up-regulation of ribosome biogenesis in cancer tissues.
source: Furthermore, two major human tumor suppressor proteins, pRB and p53, have been shown to repress the production of rRNA and the loss of these factors cause an up-regulation of ribosome biogenesis in cancer tissues, consistent with a close relationship between cancer and ribosome synthesis (Montanaro et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Up-regulation of ribosome production in cancer cells implies an enhanced dependency on QC mechanisms that survey ribosome assembly.
source: Up-regulation of ribosome production in cancer cells implies an enhanced dependency on QC mechanisms that survey ribosome assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased ribosome production in cancer cells.

claim: Huwe1 is overexpressed in multiple human tumors.
source: Interestingly, several observations link Huwe1 function to cancer. Huwe1 is overexpressed in multiple human tumors, is essential for proliferation of a subset of tumors (Adhikary et al., 2005), and is required for activation of Myc-inducible target genes including ribosomal proteins in colon carcinoma cells (Peter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Huwe1 is essential for proliferation of a subset of tumors.
source: Interestingly, several observations link Huwe1 function to cancer. Huwe1 is overexpressed in multiple human tumors, is essential for proliferation of a subset of tumors (Adhikary et al., 2005), and is required for activation of Myc-inducible target genes including ribosomal proteins in colon carcinoma cells (Peter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Huwe1 is required for activation of Myc-inducible target genes including ribosomal proteins in colon carcinoma cells.
source: Interestingly, several observations link Huwe1 function to cancer. Huwe1 is overexpressed in multiple human tumors, is essential for proliferation of a subset of tumors (Adhikary et al., 2005), and is required for activation of Myc-inducible target genes including ribosomal proteins in colon carcinoma cells (Peter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Accumulation of unassembled ribosomal proteins would titrate Huwe1, resulting in reductions in both Myc activity and transcription of genes that encode ribosomal proteins.
source: Our data suggest the intriguing hypothesis that accumulation of unassembled ribosomal proteins would titrate Huwe1, resulting in reductions in both Myc activity and transcription of genes that encode ribosomal proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.
